nm_north_rd_west.blurb: A small streambed boulder spot in the wash of Pueblo Canyon, right in the town of Los Alamos at roughly 7,200 feet. Around twenty problems sit on high-friction volcanic tuff: grippy and slopey where it is solid, crumbly in places, with sandy landings. Most lines are easy to moderate, running from the very easiest up to about V4, with a handful of harder problems into V5 and V6. A couple of short mixed or ice lines are also listed for cold winters. Plenty of holds make it good for traverses and contrived links. This is the quickest walk-in of the Pueblo Canyon areas, so it suits an after-work session, and a single pad will do.

nm_west_rock.blurb: West Rock is a compact granite outcrop in the Tres Piedras group, northwest of Taos at about 8,300 feet, tucked just north of Mosaic Rock. It holds around twenty routes, a mix of trad and bolted lines, running from easy fifth class up to low 5.11. Most of the better-known lines fall in the middle grades, with a few runout pitches, and the slabby west side is a feature. A large tree at the base gives the belayer some shade around midday. A good choice for trad climbers working through the 5.8 to 5.10 range who want quieter rock than the bigger neighbouring formations.

nm_lower_mound_western_cluster_of_boulde.blurb: The western group of boulders at U-Mound, the granite bouldering zone in the Sandia foothills on the edge of Albuquerque. Twenty problems are centred on a balancing boulder and a larger boulder beyond it, reached by a worn path from the saddle that divides this cluster from the upper clumps. The range is wide: several easy problems, a solid middle of V2 to V5, then a few seriously hard lines in the V7 to V12 range. Granite here is rough on skin, so finger-friendly technique helps. The south face of the big boulder holds the last sun of the day, making it a pleasant place to finish on a cool evening.

nm_citadel_the.blurb: A tucked-away formation in the Organ Mountains, on Rabbit Ears Canyon's western flank, east of Las Cruces, at roughly 6,400 feet. Its twenty routes are mainly traditional, with a couple of bolted lines and one top-rope, and the grades cluster from 5.7 to 5.10 with a few harder pitches at the top end and one easy line below. Some are multi-pitch ridge and corner climbs. The lower wall faces north, while other faces point west or east, so shady and sunny options are usually both on offer. Expect a long, brushy approach along the canyon, and plan on a bigger day than a roadside crag.

nm_grotto_left_east_side_lower_tier.blurb: The lower tier of the left wall in the Grotto, a shady slot within Diablo Canyon near Santa Fe, at about 6,000 feet. It is mostly bolted, with seventeen sport routes and a few trad lines, and the grading is firmly in the hard range: a couple of 5.8 and 5.10 lines, but the bulk of the climbing is 5.11 and 5.12. Expect vertical walls with sloping crimps. The rock is dense yet fractured in places, so helmets matter and so does staying out of the fall line. With a west-facing wall, it is shaded in the morning and gets afternoon sun, leaning shadier in winter and sunnier in summer.

nm_main_wall_2.blurb: The largest wall at The Dungeon, a steep volcanic-rock sport venue in the Jemez area near Los Alamos, at about 7,900 feet. Standing on the canyon's left-hand side, this big, overhanging cliff carries about twenty bolted lines with steep starts and roof sections, plus a stray boulder traverse. Nearly everything is hard: a few lines in the 5.10s, a solid block of 5.12s, and several 5.13s. Because the wall stays in shade all day, it is a sensible summer option when lower crags are too hot. Reaching it takes a half-mile walk from the parking area.

nm_muralla_grande.blurb: A towering granite face of around 800 feet in upper Chimney Canyon, below the radio towers on the Sandia crest above Albuquerque. It is the Sandias' most popular big wall for multi-pitch trad, with routes of four to seven pitches. The grades are mostly 5.8 to 5.10, with a few in the 5.11 and 5.12 range and one easy line, and the climbing is long and sustained, with some route-finding and looser rock near the tops. The wall faces southwest and stays shaded until late morning, then warms up, and it can be dry and sunny even on winter days. Expect a steep, loose gully on the way down to the base.

nm_left_side_2.blurb: The left section of the Tiger Stripe Wall near the village of Roy, in northeastern New Mexico at about 5,700 feet. Twenty sport routes make up the left half of the wall, a few of which can also be top-roped. Grades run from 5.9 up to a single 5.13, with the weight in 5.10 to 5.12. The wall sits on the canyon rim in the Middle Mesteno area above the Jumbles; reach it by the same trail down into the streambed that serves the Jumbles. It is a good stop for sport climbers who want a steady supply of 5.11 and 5.12 pitches.
